Sanctions on Jordan’s Tourism Sector Disrupt Key Sites and Spur Industry Uncertainty

Sanctions targeting Jordan’s tourism firms and the seizure of several high-profile archaeological sites have sent shockwaves through the country’s tourism industry, leaving many operators grappling with mounting losses and uncertainty. The measures, announced last week by a coalition of neighboring states over ongoing regional disputes, have resulted in the blockade of the Petra Archaeological Park and restricted access to the Wadi Rum Protected Area, both of which are managed by major Jordanian tourism agencies.

The Jordan Tourism Chamber reported a 75% drop in ticket sales at affected sites within the past five days. “We are seeing unprecedented cancellations and a severe decline in visitors,” said Hind Al-Masri, spokesperson for the chamber. “Our member firms are facing existential risks as revenues collapse and bookings vanish overnight.”

Tour operators, such as Oasis Journeys and Nabatean Trails, have suspended scheduled tours indefinitely. Local guides and site staff, many of whom are employed on a seasonal basis, have been placed on unpaid leave. According to the Jordanian Tour Guides Association, more than 4,500 workers linked to the blockaded sites have already lost wages.

Industry analysts warn that prolonged restrictions could force smaller firms into insolvency. “The Jordanian tourism sector is highly reliant on these heritage sites,” said Faisal Haddad, an Amman-based industry consultant. “If access is not restored soon, the damage to the sector’s workforce and its firms may be long-lasting.”

Government officials are in negotiations to resolve the dispute, but as of Thursday, no breakthrough had been reported. Tourism agencies say they are preparing for continued disruption as the sanctions and site seizures remain in effect.
